editorial:
True Heart Susie is a 1919 silent melodrama produced by D.W. Griffith Productions and released through Artcraft Pictures Corporation, Paramount's prestige subsidiary. Griffith directed from an original screenplay by Marian Fremont, with Lillian Gish as Susieâ€”a farm girl who secretly sells a cow to finance the education of the oblivious young man she lovesâ€”and Robert Harron as that young man, William. Cinematography was by Billy Bitzer. The film was completed before Griffith's move to United Artists and sits at the quieter, domestic end of his output, in contrast to his more contentious epics. The print passed into US public domain by term expiry: even assuming Artcraft timely registered and renewed the 1919 copyright, the maximum term under the Sonny Bono Act capped at 95 years from publication, placing expiry on January 1, 2015.

The one live rights trap is the score layer. Because True Heart Susie is a silent film, its photographic images and intertitles are free; but every home-video copy ships with a separately protected musical accompaniment. The Grapevine Video DVD carries a 70-minute orchestral score copyrighted 2007 by Film Preservationâ€”a work entirely independent of the film's expired term. A documentary maker or video essayist pulling clips from that disc and retaining its audio track would be infringing that score copyright, not the film copyright. The practical fix is to source footage from one of the score-free Internet Archive versions, or to use a CC-licensed or commissioned accompaniment and explicitly not copy the DVD audio.
faq: Can I use True Heart Susie footage commercially without a license?

The photographic contentâ€”images and intertitlesâ€”is in the US public domain and needs no license. The constraint is the music: any orchestral score added to a specific home-video copy (such as the Grapevine Video DVD's 2007 orchestral track) is a separately protected work. Source from a silent-only Internet Archive version, or confirm the copyright status of whatever accompaniment you plan to use, before including audio in your project.
Does it matter whether Artcraft Pictures renewed the copyright in the mid-1940s?

No practical effect on current US status. Even a timely renewal in 1946â€“1947 could only extend the term to the statutory ceiling of 95 years from the 1919 publication date, which expired on January 1, 2015. Renewal records are relevant if you are reconstructing the chain of title or researching foreign jurisdictions with different term rules, but they cannot extend US copyright beyond that ceiling.
